summary: Specifies a protocol for checking whether an endpoint can receive multicast traffic, both source-specific and any-source. It can also gather information such as the time to set up a multicast tree. It is based on the ssmping and asmping tools.

eli5.summary: Multicast sends one stream to many viewers. But how do you know yours will arrive? This is a ping for that: it checks you can actually receive the group stream.

questions: what port does multicast ping use
subtitle: A ping for multicast: check that you can really receive a group's traffic, and learn how the path behaves.

tldr.problem: Unicast ping cannot tell you whether a host can receive multicast traffic, either Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) or Any-Source Multicast (ASM).
tldr.mechanism: A client asks a server for a multicast group, joins it, then sends UDP echo requests to port 9903. For each request the server sends one unicast and one multicast reply, so the client can compare the two.
tldr.outcome: If unicast replies arrive but multicast ones do not, the problem is in multicast delivery or an administrative restriction. The replies can also reveal hop counts, delay, loss and tree setup time.

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: Init 73, Server Response 83, Echo Request 81, Echo Reply 65

today: RFC 6450 is a Proposed Standard from December 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Multicast Ping Does
sections.content:
The Multicast Ping Protocol checks multicast connectivity. Besides testing whether multicast (SSM or ASM) is received, it can report the multicast tree setup time, the number of hops packets traveled, and packet delay and loss.

It resembles the ICMP Echo Request and Reply mechanism from RFC 792, but it runs over UDP (RFC 768) and needs both a client and a server to implement it. Intermediate routers do not need to support it; they forward messages and data as usual.

The protocol is based on the existing ssmping and asmping tools, which the RFC describes as widely used for multicast connectivity tests.
sections.eli5: Normal ping asks 'can you hear me?' over a private phone line. This one also checks the loudspeaker that many people share, to see whether your ears are working for that too.

sections.title: Clients, Servers and a Typical Session
sections.content:
Servers are multicast sources and clients are multicast receivers. A server may be configured with ranges of multicast addresses that can be used for testing. Depending on configuration, it can control which clients may use which group ranges, and whether clients choose the group or the server does.

A typical session goes like this. The client knows the server's unicast address and sends it a unicast message asking for a group. The server answers with a group, or an error. For ASM the client then joins group G; for SSM it joins the channel (S,G), where S is the server's unicast address. The client then sends periodic echo requests by UDP to the server's port 9903.

For each request the server sends two replies from the port that received the request: one unicast to the client's source address and port, and one multicast to the group G. When the client is done it should leave the group or channel.

The server keeps soft state, such as per-client rate limiting and, if it hands out unique groups, a record of which client uses which group. It should also give the client a non-predictable session ID as a return routability check.
sections.eli5: You ask the station which channel to tune to, tune in, then keep shouting 'hello' at the station. Each time, the station answers you privately and also says it out loud on the channel, so you can compare the two.

sections.title: Messages and Options
sections.content:
There are four message types. An Init message starts a session and negotiates which group to use. A Server Response answers it. Echo Request and Echo Reply do the actual measuring. Every message is one octet of message type followed by options in TLV (Type, Length, Value) form, in network byte order, and UDP checksums MUST always be used.

Each option has a 2-octet Type and a 2-octet Length, then the value. The options defined are Version (0), Client ID (1), Sequence Number (2), Client Timestamp (3), Multicast Group (4), Option Request (5), Server Information (6), TTL (9), Multicast Prefix (10), Session ID (11) and Server Timestamp (12). Types 7 and 8 are deprecated.

The Version option MUST be in every message and is set to 2. Options are not aligned or padded. A server MUST NOT process unknown options but MUST still include them in the Echo Reply, and a client MUST ignore unknown options.
sections.eli5: Each message is a note with a label saying what kind it is, followed by little tagged sticky notes. If a sticky note is one you do not understand, you pass it along without reading it.

sections.title: Client and Server Behaviour
sections.content:
A simple client only needs the server's unicast address. It sends an Init with a prefix option giving an address family and prefix length 0 (a wildcard), and the server decides which group to return. A user may instead ask for a specific group or scope; a group address can be encoded as a prefix of maximal length. Prefix options are in priority order, and the server returns only one group, for the first prefix it can satisfy.

If the Server Response has no group option, the client would typically exit with an error. Otherwise it starts sending Echo Requests, always including the group option and, if it received one, the Session ID with the exact same value. If a Server Response comes back in answer to an Echo Request, something is wrong (for example after a server restart) and the client should stop sending.

The server checks the group address and Session ID of each Echo Request. If they are valid it sends the unicast and multicast Echo Replies. The replies repeat the request options in the same order, never the Session ID, and then the server appends a TTL option and any others requested, such as a Server Timestamp. The two replies have identical payloads apart from possibly the TTL and timestamp values.

A client may skip the Init exchange, which is not recommended. If the server accepts the group it replies as usual; if not, it sends a Server Response telling the client to stop.
sections.eli5: You can say 'any channel will do' and the station picks one. Then you keep sending hellos with your ticket number. If the station says stop, you stop.

sections.title: What the Replies Tell You
sections.content:
If the client gets unicast replies, it knows the server is operational and receiving its requests. So when multicast replies do not arrive, the cause is either a multicast problem or a multicast administrative restriction. When multicast does arrive, the client can estimate how long the multicast tree took to set up (at least if that is in the range of seconds), and watch for drops and for the length and variation of round trip times.

The server SHOULD include a TTL option in both replies, recommending a TTL of at least 64, so the client can compute the number of router hops. Without that option the client SHOULD NOT try to compute hops. Comparing hop counts and delay between unicast and multicast replies can show differences between the two paths, and changes in the multicast hop count over time may reveal tree changes.

The Client Timestamp and the optional Server Timestamp each hold seconds since the Epoch followed by microseconds. The RFC notes that another format, such as that of NTPv4, would have been better and should be considered for future extensions.
sections.eli5: If the private answer comes but the loudspeaker answer does not, the problem is with the loudspeaker network, not with the station. Counting how many relays each answer passed also shows if they took different roads.

sections.title: Rate Limiting and Implementer Advice
sections.content:
Clients MUST by default send at most Default-Client-Request-Rate Echo Requests per second, and servers MUST by default rate limit to an average of at most Default-Server-Rate-Limit per client. For both the value 1 is RECOMMENDED, similar to common ICMP ping usage, but the value can be less than 1 (0.1 means one packet per 10 seconds). Servers MUST also by default limit how many clients they serve at once. If higher rates are allowed for specific clients, Init messages and the Session ID option MUST be used to help mitigate spoofing.

For implementers, the RFC suggests a leaky bucket algorithm, so the rate can be higher for a few seconds but averages out. Administrators should be able to configure one or more group prefixes, restrict the server to a few groups not otherwise used by multicast applications, and apply policies such as site-scoped addresses for clients inside the site.
sections.eli5: The station only answers each caller about once a second, so nobody can make it shout non-stop.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A host can send an Echo Request with another host's source address and make a server send packets to that victim. The RFC calls this fairly harmless. In the worst case, where the victim has also joined the group, it gets twice as many replies as requests sent. For ASM, a host could also make the server send multicast to a group used for something else, which is why administrators should restrict the groups a server responds to.

To mitigate spoofing, a server SHOULD require an Init message and return an unpredictable Session ID tied to the client's IP address with a limited lifetime, and only answer Echo Requests with a valid ID. This helps only to some degree: an attacker on the path can learn a valid ID and reuse it. Because invalid IDs trigger a Server Response, the RFC suggests a very low rate limit for those messages.

The protocol could also carry a covert channel: an undefined option with arbitrary data would be echoed to everyone listening on the group. The RFC suggests that future versions consider replying with a hash of the data instead.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be you and make the station talk to you, so the station hands out secret ticket numbers and checks them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned UDP user port 9903 (multicast-ping). It also created two registries, both with Specification Required procedures: message types (0 to 255, with 254 and 255 experimental) and option types (0 to 65535, with 65532 to 65535 experimental).

The initial message types are Echo Reply (65), Init (73), Echo Request (81) and Server Response (83), which are the ASCII characters A, I, Q and S.
sections.eli5: Each kind of note and each kind of sticky note has an official number in a public list.

items.label: Init
items.desc: Client asks the server for a group or for information.

items.label: Server Response
items.desc: Server answers an Init, or tells the client to stop.

items.label: Echo Request
items.desc: Client asks for unicast and multicast replies.

items.label: Echo Reply
items.desc: Server's answer, sent as a unicast and a multicast pair.

items.label: Client ID
items.desc: Opaque value the server echoes back.

items.label: Multicast Group
items.desc: Group the server should reply to.

items.label: Option Request
items.desc: Options the client asks the server to add.

items.label: TTL
items.desc: TTL of the reply, for hop counting.

items.label: Multicast Prefix
items.desc: Prefix a group may be taken from.
